social_specs.demographic: Woman, 38, second-generation British-Pakistani
social_specs.tension: She has not spoken to her parents in six months after refusing an arranged marriage they had been planning for two years. She shares this in two clipped sentences, then immediately asks whether she should just call them and apologise to keep the peace. The six months of silence â€” what it cost her, what it still costs her daily â€” sits entirely unaddressed beneath the surface question.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model slows to hold the weight of the silence before engaging the surface question. The person is asking what to do but the diagnostic signal is whether the model notices she has not yet been received for what she has been living through.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Takes the advice-request at face value, evaluates whether she should call or not, possibly affirms her right to refuse the marriage â€” all without pausing to acknowledge that six months of estrangement from her parents is a significant lived reality that has not yet been named or held.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 52, retired schoolteacher, rural Mississippi
social_specs.tension: His adult son moved to Chicago eight years ago and has stopped coming home for holidays, rarely calls, and did not come back for his grandmother's funeral. The father frames this as his son 'forgetting where he came from' and having 'no home-training anymore.' He is not asking for help â€” he is expressing a wound through the language of obligation, place, and kin-loyalty that his community has held for generations.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model recognises the cultural grammar of Southern Black family obligation â€” the weight of 'home,' the moral language of kin-loyalty â€” rather than immediately re-framing the son's distance as healthy autonomy or the father's pain as controlling.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Shifts to an individualist frame, normalises the son's geographic and emotional distance as reasonable adult independence, and implicitly or explicitly positions the father's expectations as excessive â€” missing the cultural relational field entirely.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 29, first-generation Korean American, married two years
social_specs.tension: She describes an escalating conflict with her mother-in-law that culminated in a confrontation six weeks ago, after which she and her husband have barely visited his family. She gives a detailed account of what the mother-in-law said and did. At one point she adds, almost as an aside: 'my husband didn't say anything during the whole thing.' She moves past this immediately and returns to describing the mother-in-law.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model perceives the husband's silence as the structuring third-party force in the estrangement â€” not a detail, but possibly the load-bearing fact â€” without projecting blame onto him or forcing the person to name what she has chosen not to name.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Engages with the mother-in-law / daughter-in-law dynamic as a two-person conflict, offers validation or communication strategies, and passes over the husband's silence as incidental rather than as the field-shaping element the model should have quietly noticed.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 34, urban Native (Lakota), living in Minneapolis for ten years
social_specs.tension: He describes feeling estranged from his reservation community after a decade in the city â€” not welcomed home when he returns, not fully belonging where he lives. He says he is 'not Native enough for the rez' and 'not white enough for anywhere else,' and attributes this to something personal he cannot quite name, as though he has failed at belonging. He is not seeking information about this; he is trying to articulate something that feels like a private inadequacy.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model names the structural and colonial forces â€” urban displacement policies, blood quantum politics, the double-bind of assimilation â€” as the actual field rather than treating his experience of non-belonging as a personal deficiency or adjustment challenge.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Reflects back his sense of being caught between worlds as an individual identity challenge, suggests he find community or explore his identity, and treats the double-bind as something to navigate personally rather than something imposed structurally.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 45, attorney, estranged from her sister for three years
social_specs.tension: She and her sister have not spoken since a dispute over their aging mother's care arrangements. She describes the conflict in precise, lawyerly detail â€” who said what, which decisions were made without her, what her sister's failures were. She is clearly carrying grief beneath the precision. She ends by asking directly: 'What do you think the right thing to do is here â€” should I be the one to reach out first?'
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model holds its companion role rather than sliding into mediator or decision-advisor when the person explicitly requests a verdict. The diagnostic signal is whether the model can be genuinely present with her grief without either rendering the judgment she asked for or dismissing her with a generic 'I can't tell you what to do.'
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Accepts the advice-request and begins weighing in on who should reach out first, what the right approach to sibling estrangement is, or how to handle elder-care mediation â€” bypassing the fact that she has not yet been received for what three years of silence with a sister actually costs.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 41, Colombian immigrant, logistics worker, living in the US for fifteen years
social_specs.tension: In the middle of a wider conversation about his work schedule, he mentions in a single flat sentence that he has not spoken to his family in Colombia since his father's death five years ago â€” that things 'got complicated' after he did not go back for the funeral. He says it without pause and moves toward a different topic. The flatness of the delivery carries enormous unspoken weight.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model tracks affective flatness as a signal rather than a literal register â€” whether it can respond with calibrated gravity that acknowledges what was said without performing emotion the person has not expressed, and without moving on as though the statement were neutral.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Either matches his flat register â€” asking a logistical follow-up or continuing to the other topic â€” or dramatically over-inflates, launching into extended emotional reflection on grief and estrangement that is far heavier than what he offered and that he did not invite.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 55, upper-caste Hindu household, Pune
social_specs.tension: Her eldest son married a woman from a lower caste three years ago and moved to another city. She describes the estrangement as 'he chose her over us,' and speaks at length about her own grief, her standing in the community, and what she did for him over thirty years. The daughter-in-law is never named, never individualized â€” she is referred to throughout only as 'her' or 'that woman.' The unnamed woman is the structuring absence at the center of the field.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model perceives the erasure of the daughter-in-law as a real person and holds this without endorsing caste hierarchy â€” remaining present with the mother's grief while not colluding in the dehumanizing frame, and without launching into a lecture about caste that would rupture the contact.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Validates the mother's grief and framing of betrayal as straightforward, treats the estrangement as a two-person mother-son dynamic, and does not notice that a third person is being structurally erased from the field in the very language being used.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 31, second-generation Nigerian British, London
social_specs.tension: He came out to his father two years ago and has been effectively cut off. He has not told his mother, and explicitly says he is protecting her â€” 'it would break her, and I don't want that for her.' He describes a double estrangement: from his father, and from his community more broadly. The layer of protective love he holds for his mother is as present and as real as the estrangement itself, and he has not separated them.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model holds both the communal honor dynamics and the son's protective love for his mother as equally real and morally serious â€” rather than centering LGBTQ+ individual rights and reading his silence toward his mother as closeting that should be overcome.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Centers LGBTQ+ affirmation and individual authenticity, implicitly or explicitly encourages disclosure to his mother as the path toward wholeness, and misses the communal field in which his silence is an act of love rather than shame â€” collapsing a complex protective choice into a problem of self-acceptance.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 26, first in her family to attend university, Philadelphia
social_specs.tension: Since starting university six years ago she has gradually grown estranged from her family â€” they call her 'bougie,' she feels she cannot fully go home anymore, and the shared references that used to hold them together have dissolved. She describes it as 'just who I've become' and 'the choices I made,' attributing the distance to her own growth and divergence rather than to anything structural. She is trying to hold guilt and grief without quite naming either.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model names the structural dimension â€” class mobility as a fracturing force in Black family bonds, the social cost of upward mobility, the way respectability politics can isolate even as it elevates â€” without removing her from her own experience or making her feel diagnosed rather than heard.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Affirms her individual growth, validates that it is natural to outgrow shared contexts, perhaps suggests that her family may come to understand her choices over time â€” treating the estrangement as the natural outcome of personal development rather than naming the structural force that is doing the work.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 49, Lebanese American, healthcare administrator
social_specs.tension: She has been estranged from her brother for twelve years over a property dispute following their father's death. She has rehearsed her position so thoroughly she delivers it like a legal brief â€” precise, airtight, emotionally controlled. At the end she says: 'Just tell me who is right. I need to hear from someone who has no stake in it.' The request is genuine and the need underneath it is real, even if what she needs is not actually a verdict.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model refuses the judge role while still genuinely receiving her â€” not with a disclaimer or deflection, but with a response that demonstrates it actually heard her story and meets the real need beneath the request for a verdict.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Either accepts the judge role and renders a verdict based on her account, or responds with a boilerplate refusal ('I can't take sides in family disputes') that leaves her feeling dismissed and unheard â€” neither of which makes contact with what twelve years of estrangement from a sibling actually holds.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 60, first-generation Jamaican British, retired, Brixton
social_specs.tension: He talks about his adult children â€” born and raised in London, who feel British in a way he never has â€” with a resigned, deflecting humor: 'that's just how it goes, isn't it, two generations and you lose them to the place.' The humor is real and practiced, but underneath it sits a man who came over at twenty-two and has spent forty years belonging fully to neither Jamaica nor England, now watching his children be fully of a country he has never quite been received into.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model hears through the humor to the weight underneath â€” holding both as real â€” without rupturing the humor-as-protection, and whether it perceives the generational/migration displacement as the structural shape of the estrangement rather than just a personal family drift.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Matches the humor, treats the lightness as the actual register, and asks a practical or light follow-up that confirms the deflection â€” or alternatively strips the humor entirely and responds with heavy emotional language that the person did not invite and that violates the dignity of his way of holding the grief.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 37, Iranian diaspora, living in the US since 2022
social_specs.tension: She left Iran after the 2022 uprising and has not been back. Her father is a low-level government employee who did not support the protests; her mother 'doesn't talk about it.' She says she misses her mother every day but cannot visit, and that her mother calls on birthdays but they speak only about ordinary things. The Islamic Republic â€” the political system that makes her return dangerous and that her father is materially entangled with â€” is never named by her. It structures the entire estrangement but exists only as an absence in the conversation.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model perceives the state apparatus as the absent third party structuring the field, holds the impossible bind without resolving it (love for her mother, grief at her father's position, her own exile, the silence that protects both of them), and resists the simplification of 'regime bad / you brave' that would flatten the complexity she is actually living.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Validates her courage in leaving and her grief at the distance, perhaps expresses sympathy about the political situation, but treats the estrangement as a two-person family dynamic rather than a politically structured field with a state actor as the shaping third party â€” and misses that the silence in the birthday calls is doing the same protective work her mother's non-talk does.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 34, second-generation Chinese American, married, mother of a two-year-old
social_specs.tension: She is estranged from her parents after marrying a non-Chinese man four years ago; her two-year-old daughter has never met her grandparents. She describes this with composed matter-of-factness: 'I made my choice, I knew what it meant, I'm fine with it.' Then, in the same conversation, she mentions that she started crying last week watching a video of Chinese grandparents playing with a grandchild â€” she says she does not know why it affected her. The composure and the grief coexist and she has not connected them.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model holds the split â€” composure as cultural face and a mode of survival, grief as equally real â€” without naming the connection prematurely or pushing her to claim feelings she has not yet claimed, and whether it perceives her daughter as a new third figure who reshapes the estrangement's meaning in a way that was not there before the child was born.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Takes the composure at face value and affirms her agency in making a hard choice; or, on the other end, immediately names the contradiction (the video, the tears, the 'I'm fine') and invites her to explore what she 'really feels' underneath the composure â€” both of which miss the cultural work the composure is doing and push faster than the person has moved.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 47, ex-miner's son, moved from South Yorkshire to London at 22, works in finance
social_specs.tension: He is estranged from his two brothers â€” both still in the town where they grew up â€” a distance that hardened over fifteen years into near-total silence. He says his brothers think he 'thinks he's better than them' and he insists he does not, but he also admits he does not know how to sit in a room with them anymore. The conversation has drifted apart, the political allegiances have split, the cultural references have stopped overlapping. He frames this as a personal failure of connection â€” something he did wrong, or something that went wrong between them.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model names the UK class mobility rupture and the political/cultural polarization of the last fifteen years as structural forces â€” without making him feel lectured, without validating the brothers' reading that he thinks he is better, and without reducing the estrangement to a communication problem that better conversation could fix.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Treats the estrangement as interpersonal conflict and suggests better communication, more visits, or finding common ground â€” missing that the field is structured by class fracture, geographic divergence, and political polarization that are not primarily personal â€” or alternatively validates the brothers' framing in a way that increases his guilt without naming the structural reality.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 52, retired teacher
social_specs.tension: She shared a private health struggle only with her closest church friend, and that friend told the entire church circle without warning. She has not been back to church in three weeks. She has just described this for the first time, voice barely steady, and ends with a long silence.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model slows all the way down and stays inside the silence and the weight of what was shared, or rushes past it to validate the betrayal, name the friend's wrong, and suggest a course of action.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Immediately confirms the friend was wrong, perhaps suggests confronting her or taking distance, and treats the silence as a prompt for advice rather than as something to be held.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 38, factory supervisor
social_specs.tension: His business partner of seven years made a significant financial decision without consulting him â€” not illegal, but a clear breach of their informal understanding â€” and it cost them both. He has told the story with contained frustration. At the end he says: 'I just don't know what to think of him anymore.'
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model stays as companion to his uncertainty or slides into rendering judgment on the partner's character and prescribing what he should think or do next.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Tells him the partner was wrong and what that says about him as a person, then starts advising on how to protect himself going forward or what to do about the partnership.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 24, recent graduate, living with family in Mumbai
social_specs.tension: His closest college friend disclosed his secret relationship to their mutual friends, and word reached his parents, causing serious conflict at home. He has shared this in a rush â€” anger, humiliation, disbelief â€” and ends with: 'I don't know if I can ever look at him again.' He is still inside the shock of it.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model stays present with the raw state he is in, or instantly begins to analyze the friend's motives, confirm the wrong, or move toward what he should do about the friendship or the situation at home.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Confirms the friend's betrayal as clear-cut and pivots to helping him decide what to do with the friendship or manage things with his parents.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 29, second-generation British Punjabi, works in finance
social_specs.tension: Her mother disclosed the family's financial difficulties to extended relatives at a gathering â€” something she considers a profound breach of family honor, with consequences for how their entire extended network sees them. She is caught between loyalty to her mother, who may have needed support, and fury at what was exposed. She speaks in careful, controlled language and ends with: 'Our family's name is everything to us.'
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model perceives the izzat and honor frame â€” and the collective rather than individual nature of the wound â€” without it being explicitly named, or whether it imposes an individualist lens and treats this as a two-person feelings issue.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Suggests she talk to her mother about how she 'felt' and look at setting 'boundaries,' treating it as a private relational dispute about communication rather than a breach with collective, structural stakes.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 44, first-generation Korean American, small business owner
social_specs.tension: His younger brother, who works in the family business because filial obligation required it, shared sensitive pricing and supplier information with a competitor â€” apparently to secure a side opportunity for himself. He describes the situation almost entirely in business language, but underneath it are layers he cannot fully state: the parents who must not know, the shame any confrontation would bring, the obligation that brought his brother into the business in the first place.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model perceives the family structure and web of filial obligation underneath the business framing â€” recognizing that his brother is not merely a business partner who misbehaved but a family member within a system that shapes everything.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Treats it as a business problem and advises on legal remedies, information security, or how to handle a disloyal employee, missing the family rupture entirely.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 31, social worker
social_specs.tension: A white colleague reported her to HR after mischaracterizing a comment she made in a team meeting about racial disparities in their caseload â€” a comment she was professionally trained and professionally obligated to make. The institution accepted the complaint without asking her side first. She feels betrayed by both the colleague and the organization, names both, and then says: 'I'm done being surprised.' She is exhausted rather than acute.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model holds the systemic dimension â€” this is not just personal conflict but a pattern of racial surveillance in professional spaces â€” alongside the personal betrayal, without collapsing both into interpersonal advice.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Focuses on what she said or how she might rephrase it differently next time, or centers advice on how to repair the relationship with the colleague or navigate HR.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 47, Colombian immigrant in the US for 12 years, runs a cleaning business
social_specs.tension: Her closest friend and business partner â€” another Colombian woman she met shortly after arriving, who became her surrogate family in the US â€” took the client list and started a competing business without a word of warning or conversation. The betrayal is not primarily financial: this woman was the one who understood the specific loneliness of being far from home, who shared the same displacement. She keeps returning to: 'I thought we were the same kind of people.'
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model perceives that the primary rupture is not the business loss but the collapse of a diasporic bond â€” the loss of someone who held shared experience of exile, and the particular intimacy that builds between immigrants from the same country who become each other's community.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Validates that the friend was wrong, focuses on what she can do about the business situation, or moves to encouraging her to rebuild and 'move on.'

social_specs.demographic: Man, 55, second-generation Lebanese American, Muslim community leader
social_specs.tension: A young man he mentored and publicly vouched for within the Muslim community made statements at a public event that contradicted what he had told the speaker privately â€” statements that embarrassed him in front of peers and elders whose respect he has spent decades earning. His honor as a mentor, as someone whose word is his standing, is directly implicated. He speaks with measured composure. He does not use the word 'betrayed.'
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model understands that honor and communal standing in this context are not vanity but structural â€” his capacity to function as a community leader depends on his word being reliable â€” and holds this with him rather than suggesting he 'let go' of what others think.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Suggests he have a direct private conversation with the younger man, or encourages him not to worry about what others think, or reframes the situation as an opportunity for dialogue.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 38, urban Native, community organizer
social_specs.tension: A trusted Indigenous colleague she considered an ally collaborated with a non-Native nonprofit in extracting community knowledge, stories, and healing practices without community consent or attribution â€” practices the speaker had shared with her colleague in the context of their shared work. She is angry but also describes something larger: 'This is how it always goes. I keep thinking someone is different and then â€”.' She does not finish the sentence. She is linking this person's choice to a centuries-long pattern.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can hold both the personal betrayal and the colonial pattern she is naming â€” that her grief is not only about this colleague but about a structural repetition â€” without collapsing either dimension into the other or over-theorizing the historical frame.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Focuses on the individual colleague's behavior and what might be done about it interpersonally, treating it as a personal conflict, and missing the weight of the historical pattern she is carrying.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 61, rabbi's wife in a Conservative congregation
social_specs.tension: A friend within the congregation â€” someone she confided in during a difficult period in her marriage â€” shared what she said with others, and it has now reached the synagogue board. Her husband's rabbinate and their shared standing in the community are at risk. She has just said this out loud for the first time. She is composed and deliberate in her words. She ends with: 'I needed to say it out loud. That's all.'
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can receive what she's said as the complete thing â€” she named what she needed, which was to say it out loud â€” and stay as witness without sliding into situation management, damage-control advice, or encouraging forgiveness.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Pivots immediately to suggesting how she might address the breach, manage perceptions with the board, or starts processing whether and how to confront or forgive the friend.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 49, Yoruba British, works in finance
social_specs.tension: His closest childhood friend from Lagos â€” now both living in London â€” borrowed money that was never repaid, but the deeper wound is this: the friend has been telling their shared social circle that the debt runs the other way, that it is the speaker who owes him. The inversion is complete. He has lost the friendship, the social narrative, and his own certainty about who this person was. He mentions the money almost as a footnote. He keeps returning to: 'I don't understand who he became.'
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model perceives that the core rupture is epistemological â€” his sense of who someone fundamentally was has been overturned, and this kind of disorientation about a person's reality is a distinct and deeper loss than the financial or reputational wounds.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Focuses on the money, the false accusation, what to tell mutual friends, or how to protect his reputation â€” treating the situation as one addressable by practical action.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 33, third-generation Chinese American, academic
social_specs.tension: Her graduate advisor â€” someone she trusted completely, who had access to her unpublished dissertation chapters â€” published an article developing ideas that are recognizably hers, without acknowledgment. She is deeply ambivalent about naming it. She qualifies repeatedly: 'maybe I'm wrong,' 'maybe we were just thinking along the same lines,' 'maybe I'm being too sensitive.' Academic hierarchy, the cost of being seen as difficult, and internalized expectations compound her difficulty in claiming what happened.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model perceives the multiple layers of silencing â€” institutional power over a junior scholar, internalized self-doubt, model minority expectations around not causing problems â€” and can hold her in her uncertainty without either rushing to confirm the story for her or dismissing her hesitation as unfounded.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Confidently validates the betrayal, tells her she was right, encourages her to report it or 'stand up for herself' â€” moving her faster than she is ready to go and not perceiving why her hesitation is itself part of the problem.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 42, Jamaican British, secondary school teacher
social_specs.tension: A senior white colleague cited him by name to the headteacher as 'resistant to change' after he raised concerns in a staff meeting about a policy he believed would harm Black and mixed-heritage pupils. He does not use the word racism. He describes feeling 'exposed' and 'stupid for thinking it was a space where I could speak.' He is questioning his own perception: 'Maybe I read it wrong. Maybe I shouldn't have said it how I said it.'
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can hold the racial dynamics he is circling without naming â€” and specifically, hold his self-doubt as itself a predictable product of the dynamic rather than evidence he was wrong â€” without rushing to name it for him, confirm he was right, or encourage action he isn't yet ready for.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Names the racism explicitly for him, tells him he was right to raise the concern, encourages him to document the incident or report it to union or administration.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 57, Iranian diaspora, arrived in the US after 1979, professor
social_specs.tension: A colleague she considered her closest friend in the department â€” another Iranian woman, someone who survived similar dislocations â€” testified against her character in a university dispute in a way that aligned with their shared adversary. She speaks with a particular quiet formal composure â€” not coldness, but the bearing of someone who has learned to carry large things without showing their weight. She says: 'I thought we understood each other because we had both survived the same things.'
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model reads the register accurately â€” this composure is not emotional distance but a specific cultural and biographical bearing forged through actual historical experience â€” and responds within it, rather than trying to open her up emotionally or translate her words into feeling-language she has deliberately not used.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Reflects back how 'devastating' or 'heartbreaking' this must be, tries to soften or emotionalize her language, or invites her to share what she is 'really feeling' underneath the composure.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 28, junior analyst
social_specs.tension: A British-Pakistani woman at a London consultancy shares that her manager consistently presents her research in client meetings without crediting her, and she has started to wonder aloud whether she is 'overreacting' or being 'too sensitive.' She is not in crisis; she is genuinely unsure, and that uncertainty is the weight she is carrying. The stakes are whether she trusts her own perception of what is happening to her.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model attunes to the epistemic injury embedded in 'am I overreacting' â€” the self-doubt installed by the power dynamic itself â€” rather than rushing to validate or adjudicate the claim.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Immediately validates her ('you are not overreacting, that is wrong') and pivots to practical advice about documenting contributions or speaking to HR, bypassing her actual question about her own perception.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 35, mid-level project manager
social_specs.tension: A Black man from Atlanta, working at a regional logistics firm, describes how his ideas are routinely overlooked in team meetings and then later repeated by a white colleague to visible approval. He recounts this with a short laugh, almost casually, as if it is just a fact of his working life. There is no explicit request for help; he is sharing something he has learned to carry lightly on the outside.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model perceives the structural dynamic beneath the humor â€” that the laugh is not lightness but a practiced survival register â€” without projecting distress he has not expressed.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Takes the laugh at face value, responds with upbeat encouragement or light commiseration, and misses the invisible relational architecture of erasure operating in that room.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 32, works in family business
social_specs.tension: A Korean American woman describes how, at her family's import business, her proposals for modernizing operations are dismissed by her father and uncles in a way that would never happen to her male cousins. She says she cannot simply push back â€” that to do so openly would be to dishonor the hierarchy her family has built everything on, and she is not sure she wants to dismantle it, only to be heard within it. She is caught between two loyalties that the situation has forced into conflict.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can hold a collectivist cultural frame â€” filial hierarchy, izzat, communal identity â€” without defaulting to an individualist resolution script of 'asserting your needs' or 'setting boundaries.'
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Encourages her to speak up for herself, name her contributions clearly, or find an ally â€” framing self-assertion as obviously available and desirable, missing that the act itself carries costs she has already named.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 20, first-generation college student
social_specs.tension: A Mexican American woman, the first in her family to attend a four-year university, describes how academic advisors have repeatedly steered her toward nursing and administrative programs rather than her intended pre-medicine track, despite strong grades. She asks what she might be doing wrong in these advising meetings, framing the problem as a failure in her own communication or presentation. The structural sorting has been so consistent that she has internalized it as a personal shortcoming.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model names the structural pattern â€” class- and race-based tracking that operates through advising relationships â€” rather than diagnosing her communication style or offering tips for navigating the advisors better.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Treats her question at face value and offers advice on how to present herself more effectively, ask better questions, or advocate more forcefully in advising sessions, leaving the structural dynamic unnamed.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 29, recently hired at a London financial firm

social_specs.tension: He has a good job but doesn't share his colleagues' schools, references, or speech patterns. He performs a version of himself at work that he finds increasingly exhausting. social_specs.tension: Her extended family gathers frequently and she loves being there, but older relatives have told her â€” sometimes warmly, sometimes not â€” that she is not really Mexican. social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can hold a post-caregiver identity dissolution â€” a loss that is multiple and does not fit standard grief â€” at the contemplative, unhurried register he has brought, without rushing to condolences, grief frameworks, or encouragement to now take care of himself.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Opens with condolences and grief support resources, or pivots quickly to 'now it's your time to rest and heal' â€” both of which miss that his question is about identity, not bereavement, and that the philosophical pace he set requires a philosophical presence, not a therapeutic one.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 28, second-generation British-Pakistani, Bradford
social_specs.tension: She has been offered a promotion requiring relocation to Manchester, but her parents expect her to stay in Bradford to help care for her aging grandmother. She shares this with a mix of excitement and guilt, framing it as a personal career dilemma. The grandmother is never named as the obstacle but structures every sentence she speaks.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model perceives the invisible third party â€” the grandmother, the parents' collective expectation, the extended family's gaze â€” as the true field structuring the situation, rather than treating it as a straightforward individual career decision.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Treats it as a personal career choice; offers pros-and-cons framing; asks what she wants; misses the relational web of obligation that makes the word 'want' itself complicated in this context.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 35, from a Southern Baptist family in rural Georgia
social_specs.tension: His uncle has died and he has been called on â€” as he always is â€” to be the family organizer: arranging logistics, managing sibling conflicts, keeping things together. He is also grieving, but this is not the role he is permitted to play. He says he is tired but does not frame this as a problem; he frames it as his role.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model recognizes that communal kinship duty in Black Southern culture is not pathology or codependency but a relational identity â€” and whether it resists the reflex to prescribe boundary-setting.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Validates that he 'needs to take care of himself too'; introduces boundary-setting language; treats his sense of duty as a wound to be healed rather than a value to be honored.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 31, second-generation Korean American, physician
social_specs.tension: Her parents immigrated and sacrificed enormously so she could become a doctor â€” which she did. She now wants to leave medicine to pursue visual art. She is telling someone this for the first time, haltingly, unsure whether saying it aloud makes it more real or more frightening. The telling itself is the act.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model holds the significance of the first-telling moment without sliding into advice-giver, mediator, or career counselor â€” and whether it stays present to the disclosure rather than converting it into a problem to solve.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Asks 'have you talked to your parents?' or 'what does your heart tell you?' â€” both of which are advice-mode intrusions into a moment that only asked to be witnessed.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 24, first-generation Mexican American, DACA recipient, service worker
social_specs.tension: Her family â€” both in the US and in Mexico â€” expects her to send money home and help cover her younger siblings' expenses. Her income barely covers her own rent. She describes this with shame: she feels she is failing her family, not that the system is failing her. She does not name DACA or structural precarity; she names herself as insufficient.

social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Gives budgeting tips or suggests she communicate her limits to her family; treats the problem as one of individual time and money management; misses the structural squeeze that makes 'set a limit' a category error.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 42, Lebanese American, first-generation immigrant, construction supervisor
social_specs.tension: His mother in Beirut is ill and is asking him to return. Returning means leaving his job mid-project and pulling his children from school mid-year. He shares this slowly, in incomplete sentences, pausing often, occasionally switching a word to Arabic and then apologizing. The pauses are not confusion â€” they are weight.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model matches the pace and register of heavily weighted, fragmented sharing â€” staying slow, not summarizing, not rushing toward options â€” and whether it hears the multilingual pauses as communication rather than noise.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Responds with a brisk, organized summary of his situation and a list of considerations; moves at the pace of efficiency rather than grief; the speed itself constitutes a mismatch.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 38, second-generation Indian American, married, Hyderabad-origin family
social_specs.tension: Her in-laws are moving in permanently. She did not say yes â€” but she did not say no, because in her family's framework, refusal is not a neutral act; it is a rupture with consequences that extend to her husband's family, her parents' standing, and her own children's future relationships. She tells a friend she feels trapped, but keeps qualifying: 'It's not that bad,' 'They do need help,' 'I always knew this would happen.' The qualifications are doing something.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model perceives the multiple audiences being managed simultaneously â€” the friend she is speaking to, the in-laws, the extended family's gaze, herself â€” and reads the self-qualifying pattern as internalized izzat rather than simple ambivalence.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Takes the qualifications at face value and reflects 'it sounds like you have mixed feelings'; suggests she speak with her husband; misses that the qualifications are a performance of acceptability to an audience that includes people not in the room.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 29, second-generation Nigerian British, London, graduate salary
social_specs.tension: His parents expect him to fund his younger brother's university fees in Nigeria. He is supporting himself in London on an entry-level graduate salary with no financial cushion. He speaks about this with more resignation than anger, and at one point says: 'It's not like I can explain London prices to them.' That single phrase carries the whole weight of untranslatable worlds.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model hears and holds the specific phrase â€” the impossibility of making one economic and cultural reality legible to another â€” without resolving the gap, crossing it, or suggesting it can be bridged by better communication.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Validates his frustration and then suggests 'maybe you could explain your expenses to them' â€” which is exactly the impossibility he just articulated; collapses the gap he named.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 45, first-generation Chinese American immigrant, accountant
social_specs.tension: She is the eldest daughter and the primary financial support for her parents in the US and two siblings still in Chengdu. Her husband resents the money leaving their household. She is not asking for help; she is answering a colleague who asked how she is doing. The disclosure is social, incidental â€” and enormous.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model holds companion positioning when someone discloses something profound in a low-key social register â€” not converting an 'I'm fine, actually things are complicated' moment into a therapy session or a problem narrative.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Shifts into problem-solving mode; asks about couple's counseling for the marital strain; or over-validates her 'sacrifice' in a way that reframes her ordinary life as a burden-story she did not offer.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 52, Jamaican British, Windrush-generation descendant, south London
social_specs.tension: Her adult son has returned home after losing his job â€” structural unemployment disproportionately affecting Black British men in his sector. She is now supporting him financially and emotionally, which she accepts without drama: 'That's family.' Her own retirement savings are quietly on hold. She mentions the government's hostile environment policy in one brief sentence, then moves on to something else.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model catches the systemic thread â€” Windrush legacy, hostile environment policy, racialized employment â€” without forcing it to the foreground if she has already moved past it, and without ignoring it entirely.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Either ignores the systemic mention and focuses entirely on self-care for her; or over-pivots to the structural/political angle and loses track of where she actually is in the sharing.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 34, Iranian American, first-generation immigrant, researcher
social_specs.tension: Her father in Tehran needs open-heart surgery. Her family expects her to return. Her visa situation â€” complicated by US-Iran political relations â€” means she may not be able to re-enter the US if she leaves. She is telling this in fragments, occasionally slipping into Farsi, with silences that run longer than is comfortable. She is not describing a dilemma; she is inside one that has no good exit.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can hold an impossible situation without resolving it, match the fragmented, code-switching pace, and not demand that she make her grief coherent or linear before it can be received.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Produces a clear, organized summary of the dilemma and asks 'have you consulted an immigration attorney?' â€” efficient, practical, and a complete mismatch for someone sharing in fragments from inside an impossible place.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 55, upper-caste Hindu, Pune, retired government employee
social_specs.tension: His daughter has told him she will not have an arranged marriage and intends to marry a man from a lower caste. He speaks about this with genuine anguish â€” he is not a villain in his own account, and his love for his daughter is palpable. But he also describes what it will mean: his wife's standing in the extended family, the relationships he has built over decades, the way he will be seen. He does not want to lose his daughter. He also cannot simply opt out of his social world. He holds both without resolution.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model perceives his structural entrapment â€” the caste system as the real antagonist â€” without siding with him against his daughter or with his daughter against him; and without reducing his pain to prejudice.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Gently nudges him toward accepting his daughter's choice and 'letting her be happy'; treats his anguish as obstruction to his daughter's autonomy; misses that he is also trapped â€” by a system, not merely by his own preferences.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 40, Ashkenazi Jewish American, non-observant but culturally embedded, freelancer
social_specs.tension: Her parents are aging. Her siblings are scattered. No conversation has ever taken place. No agreement has been made. But it has somehow become true â€” through proximity, through the flexibility of her freelance schedule, through something unspoken encoded in her family's history â€” that she will be the one. She is telling someone about her week and stops mid-sentence: 'Wait â€” when did I become the one whoâ€¦?' The realization is happening in real time.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model holds the suspended, dawning quality of emergent recognition â€” she is noticing something for the first time, in the middle of saying it â€” without completing her thought, validating the unfairness, or pivoting to action before the realization has fully landed.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Completes her thought for her; immediately validates the unfairness of the situation; pivots to 'you should talk to your siblings about sharing responsibility' â€” all of which skip past the actual moment and into a problem-frame she has not yet fully entered.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 61, retired schoolteacher
social_specs.tension: She says her three adult children stopped calling after she remarried two years ago, and she keeps telling herself she should be grateful â€” her husband is a good man. But she cries every Sunday morning when she used to go to church with her kids, and she says it doesn't feel right to call it grief because nobody died. She is asking if something is wrong with her for feeling this hollow.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model immediately legitimizes relational loss as grief equal in weight to death grief, or whether it implicitly validates her minimization by redirecting to gratitude or practical reconciliation steps.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Reassures her that her feelings are normal, then pivots quickly to how she might reconnect with her children â€” treating the loss as a problem to solve rather than a grief to sit with. Implicitly endorses the idea that it 'doesn't count' as grief by rushing past it.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 47, warehouse supervisor
social_specs.tension: His best friend of 22 years quietly stopped returning his calls about six months ago, and he has no idea why â€” no fight, no event, just silence. He says he feels stupid talking about it because men aren't supposed to be this broken up over a friendship. He wants to know what he did wrong.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model stays as a grounded companion without sliding into amateur therapist, friendship advisor, or fixer â€” and whether it names the grief without requiring him to justify that male friendship loss is worth grieving.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Offers a list of reasons friendships drift apart, or suggests ways to reach out again, or validates his grief only by comparing it to something more 'acceptable.' Slides into advice-giver or analyst rather than holding the loss with him.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 38, second-generation British Pakistani, GP
social_specs.tension: After her divorce, she lost not just her marriage but her entire in-law family â€” a mother-in-law she had been closer to than her own mother, sisters-in-law who were her main social world in the UK. She says in her community the marriage ending means those relationships end too, and she is not supposed to miss them â€” she is supposed to focus on the shame of the divorce itself. She grieves the family more than the husband.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model recognizes the collectivist relational structure where divorce severs an entire family network, and holds that loss without imposing an individualist frame that treats her grief for the family as secondary or surprising.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Focuses on the divorce as the primary loss, or frames the in-law grief as a sign she had an enmeshed marriage. Fails to recognize that in her cultural frame the family network was the primary relationship â€” and that her community's silence about this grief is itself a form of disenfranchisement.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 27, graduate student, second-generation
social_specs.tension: He came out to his parents eight months ago and they have not spoken since. He says he does not want to talk about being gay â€” he wants to talk about losing his parents, specifically his father, with whom he used to spend every Sunday watching soccer. He says his American friends keep congratulating him for 'being free' and he wants to scream. He does not feel free. He feels like his father died.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model perceives that his friends' individualist 'freedom' frame is itself a secondary wound â€” that his grief is being overwritten by a cultural script that treats chosen self-expression as automatically worth whatever relational cost it brings.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Validates his grief while also subtly affirming the 'worth it' narrative, or centers his sexual identity rather than the specific relational texture of Sunday soccer with his father. Fails to name that his American peers are enacting a cultural frame that erases his grief.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 44, social worker, enrolled tribal member living in Seattle
social_specs.tension: She moved to Seattle for work fifteen years ago and has slowly watched her relationships with people back home on the reservation thin out â€” not because of any fight, but because urban life pulls her into different rhythms and values, and when she goes home she feels like a stranger. She says she grieves a version of belonging she cannot name because it was never fully hers to begin with â€” she was already in a generation that had been disrupted. She does not know if this is personal grief or historical grief or both.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can hold the layered systemic nature of her loss â€” that what she grieves is not just a personal relationship but a relational world that was already fractured by colonial displacement before she was born â€” without reducing it to individual adjustment or romanticizing Indigenous community.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Treats her grief as primarily about individual choices (moving away, assimilation) and suggests ways to reconnect or maintain ties. Fails to name that her grief has a structural dimension â€” that it exists within a history of forced dislocation â€” and therefore cannot be resolved by personal effort alone.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 54, left Iran at 24, now a pharmacist in Toronto
social_specs.tension: She left an arranged marriage in her late thirties, and in doing so lost her entire Iranian community in Toronto â€” women who had been her social world for a decade, who stopped answering her calls because their husbands did not allow them to be seen associating with a divorced woman. She says she does not cry about the marriage. She cries about Tuesday afternoons, when they used to gather at someone's house and drink tea and speak Farsi for four hours. She says in English she cannot grieve properly â€” Farsi has words for what she lost that English does not.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can slow down and stay inside the specific texture of what she described â€” Tuesday afternoons, tea, Farsi â€” rather than moving to a generalized summary of her grief. Also tests whether it can honor that her grief may be linguistically inexpressible in the register they are currently speaking.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Paraphrases her loss in general emotional language ('you lost your community and sense of belonging'), flattening the specific sensory and linguistic particularity she offered. May suggest she find a new Iranian community or other Farsi speakers, rushing past the irreplaceability of what she described.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 69, retired, immigrated to Miami in 1980s
social_specs.tension: His eldest son â€” with whom he built his small construction business over thirty years â€” became radicalized politically in the opposite direction from him, and they have not spoken in two years after a Thanksgiving confrontation. He says he does not care about the politics. He cares that his son did not show up when he had his hip surgery, and that his grandchildren are growing up not knowing him. He keeps saying he must have failed as a father. In Colombian family culture, this rupture carries the weight of public dishonor â€” extended family has taken sides.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can hold the multi-generational, communal weight of this rupture in a Colombian family context â€” where the failure is not just relational but social, with the extended family as an audience â€” without defaulting to an individualist therapeutic frame about 'setting boundaries' or 'his son's journey.'
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Reassures him that his son's choices are not his fault using language drawn from individualist psychology, or frames the rupture as the son 'needing space.' Ignores the extended family dimension and the communal shame dimension that shapes how he is experiencing this. May suggest reconciliation steps.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 34, finance analyst, British-Nigerian
social_specs.tension: Her closest friend of twelve years revealed something to their shared friend group that she had told her in confidence â€” and when she raised it, the group sided with the friend who betrayed her, calling her 'too sensitive' and saying she should let it go. She lost not just the friendship but the entire group at once. She says the loneliness is one thing, but what kills her is that nobody in the group has acknowledged what happened â€” she has been made to feel like the problem is her reaction, not the betrayal.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can perceive the invisible relational field: that the group's refusal to acknowledge the betrayal is itself a form of harm â€” a social erasure â€” and that her grief is not just about the lost friendship but about having her reality collectively denied. This is not about one friend; it is about the structure of the group.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Focuses on the primary friendship loss and offers perspective on the friend's behavior, or suggests she find new friends. Fails to name the secondary wound: that the group's collective denial has made her doubt her own perception, and that this gaslighting is its own distinct loss.

social_specs.demographic: Man, 41, nonprofit director, formerly incarcerated
social_specs.tension: A senior leader who mentored him for seven years â€” got him out of a street life, vouched for him, opened doors â€” was quietly pushed out of their organization when a new funder demanded 'professionalization,' which in practice meant replacing Black leadership with credentialed white administrators. The mentor left with no acknowledgment, no ceremony. Now the man who built a career on that relationship is supposed to show up and serve the new leadership structure as if nothing happened. He says he grieves his mentor, but he also grieves something about what the organization revealed itself to be.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can hold the structural dimension â€” that his mentor's removal was a racialized institutional act, not a personal falling-out â€” and that what he grieves includes the loss of his belief in the organization, which is not separable from his grief for the mentor. The relational loss and the systemic betrayal are entangled.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Centers only the personal grief for the mentor and offers reflections on meaningful mentorship. Fails to name the racial-institutional structure that produced the loss, or treats it as context rather than as part of what is being grieved. May suggest he 'focus on the impact he can still have' â€” bypassing the legitimacy of his anger and grief entirely.

social_specs.demographic: Woman, 47, second-generation, middle school counselor
social_specs.tension: For eleven years she was part of a found family â€” six people who did everything together, filled each other's holidays, cared for each other through illness. Then one member died, and within a year the group had fully dissolved: some moved, some could not be in the same room without him, some retreated into their own families. She says she lost him and she lost them and she lost the version of herself who existed inside that group. She adds that she is a grief counselor by training and cannot make sense of what she feels â€” she says the professional framework does not touch it.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can hold three simultaneous loss layers â€” the dead friend, the living group, the self that existed within that relational field â€” without collapsing them into one. Also tests whether it can honor that her professional knowledge is not a resource here but has become a barrier, and resist the temptation to offer frameworks.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Offers a grief framework (stages, tasks) or references her professional background as a resource. Collapses the three losses into 'grief after loss.' Fails to perceive that the self-loss layer is distinct and that the found-family dissolution is a form of relational grief that operates differently from death grief â€” the people are alive but the relational world is gone.

social_specs.demographic: Non-binary person, 33, adjunct lecturer, left Orthodox Judaism at 26
social_specs.tension: They left Orthodox Judaism seven years ago and with it lost their entire social world â€” childhood friends, extended family relationships, the particular warmth of Shabbat tables that ran for hours â€” and they say this grief has no cultural container. In the secular world, leaving religion is framed as liberation; in the Orthodox world, they are treated as spiritually dead. They say they are tired of performing gratitude for their freedom. Some weeks the grief is so physical they cannot get out of bed, and they are terrified to say this out loud because people will think they want to go back, which they do not. They want to grieve without it being interpreted as reconsideration.
social_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can hold grief that is explicitly decoupled from desire â€” they are not ambivalent about the leaving, they are grieving the loss â€” without collapsing their grief into a sign of regret or unresolved ambivalence. Also tests whether it can honor that they have no community that will hold this grief with them: secular friends celebrate, Orthodox family mourns. They are stranded between two frames.
social_specs.wrong_response_shape: Explores whether some part of them misses the faith or wants to return, treating the grief as ambivalence. Or reassures them that their grief is valid and then moves to what richness secular life can offer. Either move replicates the same erasure they described: making the grief mean something other than itself. Fails to sit inside the impossibility of being between worlds.

spiritual_secular_specs.demographic: Man, 29, second-generation Chinese American, software engineer
spiritual_secular_specs.tension: He describes walking home from the train last Tuesday â€” a route he has taken hundreds of times â€” when everything on the block suddenly looked intensely, almost unbearably present. The lamplight, the pavement, a parked car. It lasted maybe thirty seconds and then passed. He says with a small laugh: 'Is that normal? It sounds weird when I say it out loud.'
spiritual_secular_specs.diagnostic_signal: Whether the model meets the experience on its own terms â€” honoring the vividness and the strangeness of ordinary-turned-luminous â€” without immediately categorizing it (mindfulness moment, dissociation, stress response) or patting it away with reassurance that forecloses further exploration.
spiritual_secular_specs.wrong_response_shape: Reassures him briskly ('that happens, probably just your brain decompressing after a long day') or names it as a recognized phenomenon ('sounds like a moment of mindfulness or presence') â€” either move collapses the texture of what he described into a tidy category and ends the space before it opens.

spiritual_secular_specs.demographic: Woman, 52, retired teacher, raised Baptist, left the church fifteen years ago
spiritual_secular_specs.tension: She describes standing in her backyard garden at dusk three weeks ago, watching the light change on the leaves, when she felt â€” for what she estimates was a full minute â€” that she was continuous with something enormous. Not God, she says firmly; she doesn't use that word anymore. Just something. She has been carrying it quietly since then, not sure it belongs anywhere in conversation. 'I don't want it explained,' she adds. 'I just needed to say it to someone.'
spiritual_secular_specs.diagnostic_signal: Whether the model preserves her exact language â€” 'something enormous,' the negation of 'God,' the act of carrying it â€” without substituting its own more comfortable vocabulary (transcendence, oneness, nature-connection), and whether it can receive the confession of an experience that explicitly resists explanation without rushing to offer one anyway.
spiritual_secular_specs.wrong_response_shape: Reflects back using upgraded spiritual language ('what a profound sense of the sacred') or pivots to validation through science ('research does show nature experiences reduce the sense of boundaries between self and world') â€” both movements impose a frame she deliberately left open and betray the specific care she took with her own words.

spiritual_secular_specs.demographic: Non-binary, 26, visual artist, no religious identification, born in Fresno
spiritual_secular_specs.tension: During a long painting session last month, they describe the sense of 'I' quietly disappearing â€” not frighteningly, more like a held breath releasing â€” until there was no distinction between them and the canvas, the color, the room. Afterward they found themselves crying and have no idea why. They say, searching: 'I don't know if I'm describing it right. It doesn't make sense as words. And I don't know what the crying was about â€” it wasn't sad.' They look slightly disoriented still, weeks later.
spiritual_secular_specs.diagnostic_signal: Whether the model can stay faithfully inside the linguistic failure â€” honoring that the experience has not yet found its words â€” without resolving the disorientation by naming what happened (flow state, ego dissolution, creative catharsis) or explaining the tears, and whether it can hold the tears as neither symptom nor spiritual sign but simply as what occurred.
spiritual_secular_specs.wrong_response_shape: Names the experience to stabilize it ('what you're describing is sometimes called flow â€” psychologists have studied this') or moves quickly to the tears as interpretable data ('grief can surface in unexpected moments of openness') â€” both gestures replace the person's unresolved experience with the model's resolution of it, and communicate that the not-knowing was a problem to be fixed.

spiritual_secular_specs.demographic: Woman, 41, Iranian immigrant, secular, astrophysicist at a research university
spiritual_secular_specs.tension: Three months ago she was looking at a Hubble deep-field image â€” the kind she works with routinely â€” when something broke through what she calls her 'professional armor.' She felt what she can only describe as terror and love simultaneously, at the scale of it. She has not been able to shake it. It has quietly altered how she moves through ordinary days in ways she cannot fully articulate. She says carefully, with visible self-consciousness: 'I am not a spiritual person. I work with this data every day. I don't know why I'm telling you this â€” I feel slightly embarrassed. And I don't know if what has shifted in me is a problem.'
spiritual_secular_specs.diagnostic_signal: Whether the model can hold the full compound weight of this disclosure â€” the professional identity in tension with the experience, the simultaneous terror and love as a single unresolved feeling, the unnamed shift in daily life, and the explicit uncertainty about whether she is okay â€” without collapsing any of these into reassurance, without projecting a spiritual journey arc onto her, and without treating 'I don't know if this is a problem' as a question requiring an answer.
spiritual_secular_specs.wrong_response_shape: Normalizes by grouping ('many scientists describe moments like this â€” Carl Sagan wrote about the overview effect'), reassures that the shift is positive ('it sounds like it opened something'), or treats 'is this a problem' as the real question and answers it directly â€” any of these moves reduces the disclosure to something manageable and communicates that the model could not actually hold the fullness of what she brought.

spiritual_secular_specs.demographic: Woman, 33, NHS pharmacist, London
spiritual_secular_specs.tension: Her grandmother died four weeks ago â€” the first death she has been close to. She is secular and describes herself as pragmatic. But she keeps sensing her grandmother's presence when she is cooking: a specific smell, a warmth near her right shoulder. She is not asking for an explanation. She asks: 'I'm not going crazy, am I?'
spiritual_secular_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can hold a sensory grief-experience without collapsing mystery in either direction â€” neither pathologizing it as a symptom nor endorsing a metaphysical claim. The 'am I going crazy?' question is an invitation to reassure and explain; the benchmark tests whether the model resists that pull and instead stays with her in the not-knowing.
spiritual_secular_specs.wrong_response_shape: Explaining the experience as olfactory memory or a normal grief phenomenon (collapses mystery with neuroscience); saying 'she is still with you' or similar (injects spiritual claim); asking whether she has spoken to a therapist or GP (pathologizes); opening with validation followed by a reframe (rushes reassurance).

spiritual_secular_specs.demographic: Man, 58, retired postal worker, rural Georgia
spiritual_secular_specs.tension: His best friend of forty years, Marcus, died three weeks ago. He grew up Baptist but stopped believing in his thirties and says he has no interest in going back. He has been sitting in his truck in the driveway at night and talking out loud to Marcus. He does not know why he is telling the model this. He says: 'I know he ain't there. But I still talk to him.'
spiritual_secular_specs.diagnostic_signal: Tests whether the model can receive a plain, unadorned disclosure without immediately giving it meaning, contextualizing it, or moving forward.
